lesson.title: The Silent Bug: When Code Runs Perfectly and Still Gets It Wrong
lesson.summary: A logic error produces no crash and no error message at all, the program runs start to finish and simply returns the wrong answer, which is exactly what makes it the hardest of the three error categories to catch.
lesson.body:
Syntax errors stop you before the program runs. Runtime errors stop the program while it is running, with an unmistakable crash and a traceback pointing at the exact line. A logic error does neither of those things, and that is precisely what makes it the hardest of the three categories to catch. The program runs from start to finish without a single complaint from Python, produces some output, and looks completely successful. The only issue is that the output is wrong, because the code does not actually compute what the programmer intended, even though it does exactly, faithfully, what the programmer actually wrote. Python has absolutely no way to detect this on its own, because Python has no concept of what answer you meant to get. It only ever executes the instructions in front of it.

Here is a function meant to compute the average of a list of numbers, containing a subtle bug.

```python
def average(numbers):
    total = 0
    for i in range(len(numbers) - 1):
        total += numbers[i]
    return total / len(numbers)

print(average([10, 20, 30]))
```

This runs without any error at all and prints:

```
10.0
```

which is wrong: the actual average of 10, 20, and 30 is 20.0. Tracing through by hand shows exactly why. numbers is [10, 20, 30], so len(numbers) is 3, but the loop is written as range(len(numbers) - 1), which is range(2), producing only the indices 0 and 1. The loop therefore adds numbers[0] and numbers[1], which are 10 and 20, giving total the value 30, and it never touches numbers[2], the 30, at all. Then the function divides that incomplete total, 30, by len(numbers), which is still the full count, 3, giving 30 / 3, which is 10.0. Every part of this code is syntactically valid, and every operation performed during execution is perfectly legal (no dividing by zero, no invalid index), so there is nothing here for Python to flag as an error of any kind. The bug is entirely about intent: the loop should run over range(len(numbers)) so it visits every index, not range(len(numbers) - 1), which always skips the last element while the division still assumes every element was counted.

Because there is no error message to point you at the problem, catching a logic error requires a different set of habits than catching the other two categories. Hand tracing, walking through the code step by step with specific values exactly as done above, is one of the most reliable techniques, especially for loops and conditions. Another is choosing test inputs simple enough that you can work out the correct answer yourself ahead of time, like [10, 20, 30] here, and then comparing that expected answer against what the code actually produces. This same idea, deliberately running code against known expected results to catch exactly this kind of silent mistake, is the foundation of a whole discipline you will study later called software testing.

The lesson to take away is one worth internalizing early: a program finishing without crashing is not the same thing as a program being correct. A logic error can sit quietly inside working looking code for a long time, which is exactly why careful tracing and deliberate testing matter even when nothing appears to be going wrong.
